title: The path of the deathless (21–23)
hook: earnestness is the path to the deathless; the careless are as if dead already

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cowherd, and your line: not someone else's cows. Which verse did you live instead of reading? Day one hundred sixty-two, and chapter two begins.
screen: `OTHER PEOPLE'S COWS — NOT SOMEONE ELSE'S COWS.`

segments.voice: A car pulls into the driveway, and the driver has no memory of the drive. A bag of chips is empty by the end of the show, and only the first one was tasted. A friend gets a “yeah, totally,” and a minute later the listener has no idea what was said. Hours can pass like that. The body is there; nobody's home. Chapter two of the Dhammapada has a blunt name for that state, and a single word for its opposite. Today: the path of the deathless.
screen: `THE DRIVE YOU DON'T REMEMBER.` → `THE BODY'S THERE; NOBODY'S HOME.` → `A BLUNT NAME FOR IT.`

segments.voice: The word is appamada. It's built from pamada, which means carelessness, heedlessness, drifting, and the little prefix a-, which turns it around. So appamada is not-drifting: heedfulness, alertness, care. Müller translates it earnestness. Here's verse twenty-one in his English: “Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death. Those who are in earnest do not die, those who are thoughtless are as if dead already.” As if dead already. That's the blunt name. Not a threat about the future, but a description of the drive you don't remember. The word Müller renders immortality is amata, the deathless, one of the old names for nibbana. Verses twenty-two and twenty-three go on: the wise, who understand this, delight in heedfulness, and by steady, strong practice they reach nibbana, the highest happiness. This one word matters so much that the tradition remembers it at the very end of the Buddha's life. In the long discourse on his final days, his last words to the monks, in Rhys Davids' translation, are: “Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!” That last word, diligence, translates the same word: appamada. Some teachers say the whole teaching, at the end, is folded into it. Notice it doesn't mean rushing or straining. The heedful person isn't frantic. They're simply here: tasting the chip, hearing the friend, seeing the road. And the verse's claim is striking. In its terms, that kind of presence isn't only the path to something later. The heedful are the ones who are alive.
screen: `APPAMADA — NOT DRIFTING.` · `THE CARELESS: AS IF DEAD ALREADY.` · `AMATA, THE DEATHLESS.` · `THE BUDDHA'S LAST WORD.` · then, large: `HEEDFUL IS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Let's practice appamada with the simplest task there is: breathing. Sit, and give this breath your full attention, from the first touch of air to the last. Then the next. When you notice you've drifted, and you will, that noticing is the moment of heedfulness. It isn't a failure; it's the practice. Come back, without scolding. Later today, choose one ordinary task: brushing your teeth, washing a mug, tying your shoes, and do it with the same full attention. The bell holds the time.
Appamada. Heedfulness: the opposite of drifting. The path to the deathless, and the Buddha's last word.
Your line: heedful is alive. Today, do one task with full attention, start to finish, and notice how different it feels from doing it on autopilot. Day one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often stress appamada, heedfulness, and recall the Buddha's last words urging his followers to strive on with heedfulness.

match.prompt: match the words of chapter two.
pairs: the deathless, a name for nibbana
work out your salvation with diligence

myth: appamada means rushing and straining harder
it means not drifting: simply being present and careful, not frantic.
the Buddha's last words, in Rhys Davids' translation, end 'work out your salvation with diligence'
diligence there translates appamada, the same word as chapter two.
'as if dead already' is a threat about what happens after death
it describes the state of drifting through life with nobody home.

fork.setup: you notice, halfway through the sit, that your mind has been planning dinner for a minute. what does heedfulness look like now?
options: notice it and come back to the breath.
fork.reveal: the noticing itself is appamada. coming back, without scolding, is the practice.

original.note: Pali: heedfulness, from a- (not) and pamada (carelessness).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'earnestness' means being very serious.
what it means: appamada is not drifting: full attention, the opposite of autopilot.
what a scholar hears: the Buddha's last words in DN 16, 'appamadena sampadetha,' use the same word; Müller's 'immortality' renders amata, the deathless.

sources.quoted: Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death. Those who are in earnest do not die, those who are thoughtless are as if dead already.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Maha-parinibbana Sutta), 6.10, the last words
sources.quoted: Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!

notes: Editor review (days 151-169): hook no longer tells the listener what they did; 'same root' corrected to 'same word' (appamadena); 'whole teaching in one word' attributed to some teachers; narrator no longer states the verse's claim as fact.
Check Müller's verse 21 word for word against SBE 10.
Rhys Davids' rendering of the last words (Dialogues of the Buddha, part II, 1910): confirm exact wording and punctuation.
Commentary story for verses 21–23 (Samavati and Magandiya) is not told; the last words are used instead.
